options: Set-Cookie does not inhibit caching; this response could be stored and served to others
Set-Cookie always prevents caching
Set-Cookie makes the response private
Set-Cookie is stripped by every cache
explain: RFC 9111 section 7.3 says Set-Cookie does not inhibit caching. Some caches (nginx by default) refuse to store such responses, but you cannot rely on that; the origin must send no-store or private.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting, responding, and practising safely
question: After fixing a web cache deception bug, why must you also revoke sessions or tokens?
options: Responses already stored or fetched may have exposed tokens; purging the cache does not invalidate copies an attacker already holds
Revoking makes the cache faster
RFC 9111 requires it
It is needed to enable HTTP/2
explain: The fix and the purge stop future exposure. Anything already read by an attacker, such as the access tokens in the ChatGPT case, stays valid until revoked.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
question: With the defaults, what does setting khugepaged/max_ptes_none to 0 trade away?
options: Faults no longer allocate huge pages
khugepaged will not collapse any range with even one unpopulated PTE, so sparse regions stay on 4 KiB pages but never bloat
Huge pages can no longer be swapped
khugepaged stops running
explain: max_ptes_none only governs collapse: at 0, a range must have all 512 PTEs populated. That removes collapse-induced bloat but fewer ranges become huge. Fault-time allocation is controlled by enabled and defrag, not this knob.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Measure recall yourself: MQAR and a tiny hybrid in code
question: Why does MQAR separate a recurrent model from attention more sharply than a test with a single query at the end?
options: A single query lets the model store little; with many queries at different times, every pair must stay retrievable at once
MQAR sequences are much longer, and recurrent models cannot run on long sequences
MQAR uses a larger vocabulary, which recurrent models cannot embed
With one query, attention cannot find the key
explain: With one question at the end, a recurrent model can in principle get by with whatever survived in its state. MQAR asks about every pair, in an order the model cannot predict, so all of them must be held simultaneously in the fixed state. Attention just looks each one up.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
question: A team must cut KV memory but keeps exact recall at 200K tokens. Which design is riskiest?
options: 1 full attention layer per 8 layers, Mamba-2 elsewhere
Mamba layers plus only 2048-token sliding window attention
Gated DeltaNet with a full attention layer every 4 layers
Parallel attention and SSM heads with global attention in the first, middle and last layers
explain: With only sliding window attention, no layer can look up a token 200K positions back exactly; that recall must survive inside the fixed Mamba state. The other three keep at least a few global attention layers that can read the whole KV cache.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Convex combination: normalize, then weight with alpha
question: After min-max normalization, a query whose dense results all have cosine 0.80 to 0.81 gets dense scores spread from 0 to 1. What is the risk?
options: None; normalization makes scores comparable by design
Cosine scores become negative
Tiny, possibly meaningless cosine differences are stretched to the full range and can outweigh real BM25 differences
BM25 scores are rescaled to match the cosine range
explain: Min-max always maps the list's min to 0 and max to 1, regardless of how close they were. Our toy shows a milder version: a 0.11 cosine range became 0 to 1. Theoretical min-max (dividing from the known lower bound, -1 for cosine) keeps such near-ties close.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
question: You normalize the HyDE mean vector to length 1 before searching an inner-product index. What happens to the top-10 results?
options: They stay the same; only the score values change
They change, because longer vectors favor longer documents
They improve, because cosine is always better than inner product
They get worse, because the query contribution is removed
explain: Dividing the query vector by its positive length scales every document's score by the same factor, so the ordering is identical. Document vectors are untouched, so this is not the same as switching the whole index from inner product to cosine.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Inside a plant: sensors, PLCs, RTUs, HMIs, historians and SIS
question: A refinery's safety system is designed so that it can still shut the unit down even if the main control system has crashed. Which design property is this?
options: Redundancy of the historian
Independence of the SIS from the BPCS
Real-time scheduling of the HMI
Remote access to field sites
explain: NIST describes the SIS as often independent from other control systems so that a BPCS failure does not harm SIS function. That independence is exactly what attackers in the Triton case worked to get around.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Modbus/TCP byte by byte, and why it trusts everyone
question: A server replies with function code 0x83 and one data byte 0x02. What happened?
options: A successful read of 2 registers
A new function code 0x83 the server supports
A write of value 2
An exception to a Read Holding Registers (03) request, with exception code 2
explain: Exception replies set the high bit: 0x80 + 0x03 = 0x83. Exception code 02 is 'illegal data address' in the spec. A burst of exceptions often means someone is probing addresses.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Ukraine 2015 and Industroyer 2016
question: Why did ESET judge Industroyer more dangerous than the 2015 toolset?
options: It encrypted files for ransom
It was signed with stolen certificates
It spread by USB
It implemented four industrial protocols itself, so it could command switches and breakers directly without the operators' software
explain: ESET: the authors 'went to great lengths to create malware capable of directly controlling switches and circuit breakers', speaking IEC 101, IEC 104, IEC 61850 and OPC DA. A tool like that can be reused at other utilities with the same protocols.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Watching OT: asset inventory and passive monitoring
question: The Suricata Modbus rules never fire, even in a test with real write traffic. What is the most likely cause?
options: Modbus writes cannot be detected
Suricata needs encryption keys
The sid numbers are too high
The Modbus app-layer parser is disabled by default in suricata.yaml, so 'alert modbus' rules have nothing to match
explain: Suricata ships with the Modbus parser disabled. Enable it and set detection port 502; its docs also advise unlimited stream reassembly depth for long-lived Modbus connections.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Inside a SAML response: Issuer, Subject, Conditions and statements
question: An assertion for `https://payroll.example.com` is presented, within its time window and with a valid signature, to `https://wiki.example.com`. What should the wiki do?
options: Accept it, since the IdP signed it
Accept it but log a warning
Reject it: its AudienceRestriction does not name the wiki
Forward it to the payroll app
explain: The Audience says which SP the IdP meant the statement for. A genuine signature only proves who issued it. Accepting another SP's assertion would let any app that receives assertions log in as its users elsewhere.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Case: ruby-saml CVE-2024-45409 and the GitLab SAML bypass (2024)
question: Why did enabling MFA at the IdP not protect GitLab instances from CVE-2024-45409?
options: The IdP's MFA was too weak
GitLab ignores IdP MFA by design
The forged response was presented directly to GitLab; the IdP was never asked to authenticate anyone
The flaw was in the IdP
explain: An SP-side verification bypass means the attacker constructs the response and posts it to the SP. Controls that live at the IdP never run. GitLab's mitigation was a second factor at GitLab itself.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: SCIM provisioning: creating and removing accounts in every app
question: A company uses JIT provisioning only. Ana leaves and is disabled at the IdP. What remains in each app?
options: Nothing: JIT accounts are deleted at logout
Only Ana's email address
Ana's app account, with whatever data and API keys it holds, because the app is never told Ana left
A SCIM error
explain: JIT creates accounts on login and hears nothing on departure. The account and anything attached to it stay until someone removes them, which is why push provisioning or regular access reviews are needed.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Case: Okta's support system and the stolen HAR files (2023)
question: Which control would have made the stolen HAR session tokens fail when replayed from the attacker's network?
options: A stronger password policy
Longer session lifetimes
Binding admin sessions to the network (ASN) they were created on, so reuse from elsewhere forces reauthentication
Encrypting HAR files at rest in the support system
explain: The tokens were valid sessions; passwords were never involved. Okta's remediation was exactly session binding for admins. Encrypting files at rest would not help against an actor using a legitimate service account that can read them.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Leavers: deprovisioning, SCIM and the Cash App download
question: Block's filing says the former employee had regular access to the reports in a past role, and used it after leaving. Which control most directly addresses that failure?
options: Stronger password rules for employees
Removing every entitlement, including in tools with local accounts, at termination, then reconciling to catch misses
Encrypting the reports at rest
Requiring employees to sign a non-disclosure agreement
explain: The access itself outlived the job. Complete deprovisioning, including applications outside single sign-on, and reconciliation to catch what was missed, address that directly. Encryption at rest does not stop an authorised account from reading data.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Privileged access: why admin rights differ, and the Snowden case
question: Ana is a domain administrator who also reads email and browses the web all day on the same account. Which NIST control does this break, and why does it matter?
options: AC-6(2): privileged users should use a non-privileged account for non-security work, so a phishing email does not land on an admin account
PS-4: Ana has not left the company
AC-2(3): Ana's account is not dormant
IA-5(7): there is no embedded password
explain: AC-6(2) separates everyday work from admin work. If the account that opens attachments is also a domain admin, any malware it runs starts with domain admin rights.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Just-in-time admin and break-glass accounts
question: A tenant makes every Global Administrator and Privileged Role Administrator assignment eligible, requires approval to activate, and the only approvers have left the company. What happens, and what prevents it?
options: Activation is approved automatically after 24 hours
Nobody can activate, so administration is locked; tested break-glass accounts with permanently active rights prevent it
HR can approve activations instead
The eligible users become active automatically
explain: Microsoft documents this exact lockout. Its emergency access guidance makes break-glass accounts permanently active Global Administrators, outside the approval flow, protected by phishing-resistant credentials and alerting.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Solving for a homography with the DLT, by hand
question: You pick four matches for the DLT, but three of them lie on one straight line. What happens?
options: The DLT still works because 8 equations are enough
SVD returns the identity matrix
The fourth point is automatically ignored
The solution is degenerate: A loses rank and H is not determined
explain: Collinear points do not pin down the projective map; the system has a bigger null space and many H fit. OpenCV's findHomography docs say its robust methods discard collinear 4-point subsets for this reason.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Events, alerts and incidents: when does it become an incident?
question: Antivirus in monitor mode logs that Mimikatz ran on a finance PC. Nothing else is known yet. What is the best classification?
options: An incident: unauthorised code ran, so integrity is already jeopardized
A routine event, because the tool did not block anything
An adverse event to keep watching, with no declaration until data is lost
A false positive until a second tool confirms it
explain: The NIST definition covers occurrences that actually or imminently jeopardize integrity or confidentiality. Credential-dumping code running on a host already does. Waiting for data loss is how the HSE detection on 31 March became a nationwide outage on 14 May.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Containment: isolate, watch, disable, block, and the trade-offs
question: Which is the strongest reason NIST gives against prolonged "watch the attacker" containment?
options: The attacker can escalate access or compromise other systems while you watch, and the organisation may be liable
It is illegal everywhere
It produces too much log data
Attackers always notice monitoring
explain: NIST calls delayed containment dangerous because the attacker could escalate unauthorised access or compromise other systems, and recommends discussing any sandbox strategy with legal first.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Windows artefacts: event logs, Prefetch, Amcache, Shimcache, MFT
question: A suspicious EXE appears in Shimcache, and nowhere else: no Prefetch file, no 4688 event, no EDR record. What can you conclude?
options: It definitely ran
Shimcache is unreliable, so ignore it
It existed on the host at some point, but execution is not proven
The attacker must have deleted the Prefetch file
explain: Shimcache can record files that were present but not executed. Treat it as evidence of presence and look for other execution artefacts before concluding it ran.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Eradication and recovery: rebuild, credentials, krbtgt and backups
question: Why does Microsoft say to reset the krbtgt password twice, with at least 10 hours in between?
options: The account keeps the two most recent passwords; the second reset removes the stolen one from the history, and the wait lets legitimate tickets expire normally
The first reset often fails silently
Domain controllers replicate only on the second change
Ten hours is how long a reset takes to replicate
explain: With a history of two, the stolen key is still in the history after one reset; the second reset pushes it out. The wait matches the default maximum ticket lifetime (10 hours), so tickets issued before the first reset have expired first.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Blameless postmortems, lessons learned and tabletop exercises
question: A postmortem says: "Root cause: the on-call analyst ignored the alert." Why would a blameless review reject this as the conclusion?
options: Because it names a person and stops there; the review should ask why the alert was easy to miss (volume, routing, ownership, monitor mode) and fix that
Because analysts never make mistakes
Because alerts are not part of IR
Because only executives can be named
explain: Blameless reviews look for systemic causes. If one tired person could miss it, the next one can too; the fix is in the system (alert design, ownership, staffing), which NIST r3 calls the underlying or systemic root cause.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Beyond the login: UNION, blind and second-order injection
question: A search page shows no results and catches every database error, but it responds about five seconds slower for some inputs. What does this suggest?
options: Nothing: without visible output, SQL injection cannot be exploited
A UNION attack, since UNION queries are always slower
A cross-site scripting bug
Possible time-based blind injection: response time can leak whether an injected condition is true
explain: Blind injection needs only an observable difference. Time is observable. If an injected condition can make the query pause, the attacker learns one bit per request, and tools can repeat that thousands of times.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: ORMs, stored procedures and least-privilege accounts
question: A Java app calls a stored procedure with `prepareCall("{call find_user(?)}")` and `setString(1, input)`. Inside, the procedure builds a query with `'... WHERE name = ''' + @name + ''''` and runs it with EXEC. Is the app safe from SQL injection?
options: Yes, because the call uses a placeholder
Yes, because stored procedures cannot be injected
No: the input arrives safely as a value, but the procedure pastes it into new SQL text and runs it
No, because CallableStatement does not support parameters
explain: Binding protects the call, not the dynamic SQL constructed inside the procedure. The fix is inside the procedure: bind the value in the dynamic query (sp_executesql with parameters in SQL Server, EXECUTE ... USING in PostgreSQL) or avoid dynamic SQL.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Shellshock: when an environment variable became code
question: A Python CGI script, not a bash script, runs `os.system("/usr/bin/uptime")` with no user input in the command. Was it exposed to Shellshock on a server with vulnerable bash as /bin/sh?
options: No: the command contains no user input
Yes: os.system starts a shell, which inherits the HTTP_ variables from CGI and parses them at startup
No: Python scripts are immune
Only if the script was run as root
explain: The attacker's data is in the environment, not the command line. os.system runs /bin/sh -c, and a vulnerable bash as /bin/sh imports function-like variables at startup and runs the trailing code.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: The defence map: validation, encoding, parameters and detection
question: Your PostgreSQL log suddenly shows dozens of `permission denied for table users` errors from the web application's account. What is the most likely explanation and first step?
options: Normal behaviour; ignore it
A disk failure; restore from backup
Something, possibly injected SQL, is asking for data the app was never granted; find the requests behind it in the access logs and treat it as a likely attack
The password column is corrupted
explain: A correct application never queries tables it lacks rights to, so these errors usually mean a bug or injection probing. Least privilege stopped the read; correlate timestamps with web logs to find the endpoint and input.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
question: A configuration service does about 50 small reads per second in short bursts, on a 2-core VM that is already busy. A teammate proposes `IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL` to save system calls. Good idea?
options: Yes, SQPOLL always lowers latency
Yes, but only with IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL as well
No: at 50 I/O per second the syscalls saved are negligible, and the poll thread competes for one of only 2 busy CPUs and keeps going to sleep between bursts
No, because SQPOLL requires root on all kernels
explain: SQPOLL pays off when a stream of submissions keeps the thread busy. Here it would mostly spin or sleep and wake, costing CPU on a constrained machine for almost no saved work. Privilege is no longer required on recent kernels, so that is not the reason.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Gadgets: from a polluted prototype to code execution (Kibana)
question: After upgrading to a Node.js release that includes pull requests 48726 and 53781, a team decides their unpatched deep-merge helper is no longer a risk. Why is that wrong?
options: The pull requests hardened only Node.js's own child_process option handling; other gadgets in frameworks, libraries and the app still read polluted properties
Those changes only apply when Node.js runs with --permission
The changes were reverted because the Node.js threat model rejects them
Prototype pollution only matters in browsers, so the helper was never a risk
explain: The hardening stops child_process from reading env, shell and similar options from the prototype. Logic gadgets (isAdmin), request options, template engine options and countless library defaults are untouched. The source still has to be fixed.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: eval, new Function and why node:vm is not a sandbox
question: A SaaS (software as a service) product lets customers upload JavaScript 'rules' and runs them with `vm.runInNewContext(rule, { order })`. What is the core problem?
options: runInNewContext is slower than eval
Customers cannot use modern syntax in a vm context
node:vm is documented as not a security mechanism; shared objects such as order lead back to the host's Function constructor and from there to process
The rule cannot read order because contexts share nothing
explain: The Node.js docs say not to use node:vm for untrusted code. Anything passed in, like order, carries a constructor chain back to the host realm. Use a separate, low-privilege process or a non-code rules format.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Middleware and internal headers: the Next.js bypass
question: Why did the fix for CVE-2025-29927 generate a random ID at server start instead of simply removing the recursion check?
options: Because random IDs make the server faster
Because the header was required by HTTP/2
Because the recursion guard is still needed for the server's own subrequests; the ID lets the server prove a marker came from itself, and markers without it are dropped
Because the ID encrypts the response
explain: The guard prevents middleware from looping on the server's own inner fetches, so it has to stay. What was missing was authentication of the signal. A per-process secret known only to the server separates its own markers from forged ones.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Finding and catching JavaScript bugs: tools, signals, practice
question: After a confirmed prototype pollution incident on a Node.js API, the team deploys the fixed merge function. Which step must not be skipped?
options: Clearing the browser cache of every user
Restarting every process that ran the vulnerable code, because the polluted Object.prototype persists in memory until the process exits
Rotating the TLS certificate
Reinstalling Node.js
explain: Fixing the code stops new pollution but does not undo pollution already in a running process's heap. If a gadget reached code execution, rebuild hosts and rotate secrets as well.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
question: A latency-sensitive service shows p99 spikes every few seconds, and a profile shows time in page faults right after memory was purged. Which change targets this most directly?
options: Increase the number of size classes
Disable the thread cache
Lengthen the purge delay (jemalloc dirty_decay_ms or MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY) so freed pages stay mapped longer between bursts
Lower jemalloc's opt.narenas to 1
explain: The spikes come from returning pages to the OS and faulting them back in. A longer delay keeps them resident across bursts, at the cost of higher RSS. Disabling caches or arenas adds contention without fixing the faults.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: The nemesis: partitions, pauses, clocks and crashes
question: A coordination service hands out locks that expire if the holder misses heartbeats for 2 s. Which nemesis is most likely to show two clients holding the same lock?
options: Process pauses with SIGSTOP and SIGCONT lasting longer than the lease
A partition that isolates one follower that holds no locks
Bit flips in a log file on a single node
Packet duplication on a client link
explain: A paused holder cannot notice its lease expiring, so another client acquires the lock, and the first resumes believing it still holds it. Isolating an uninvolved follower or flipping bits does not target the lease mechanism.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Prune before you measure: shared memory and registers
question: A config that uses 144 KiB of shared memory tunes fine on a cc 9.0 GPU. The same tuning job runs on a cc 8.6 GPU and that config is now rejected. What should the tuner do?
options: Reduce num_stages automatically until it fits and keep the measured timing
Treat the limit as device state: prune against this device's limit and re-tune, because the legal space itself changed
Keep the cc 9.0 result, since the config is still correct code
Fail the tuning run, because the config list is invalid
explain: Shared memory per block is a documented per-capability quantity (227 KB at 9.0, 99 KB at 8.6), so the set of legal configurations is part of the device, not the kernel. Silently rewriting num_stages produces a config nobody measured, and carrying the old winner over is exactly the stale-cache failure of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Handing the device to user space: vfio-pci, BARs and DMA memory
question: Why do DPDK and SPDK allocate I/O buffers from hugepages rather than plain malloc memory?
options: Because NICs cannot DMA into 4 KiB pages
Because VFIO only accepts 1 GiB pages
Because hugepages are faster for the device to read over PCIe
Because hugepages have physical addresses that Linux does not move today and are contiguous within a page, and they also cut TLB misses
explain: The device must be given addresses that stay valid. Hugepages are not migrated by Linux today and each one is physically contiguous; the TLB benefit is a bonus. With an IOMMU, VFIO pins and maps them explicitly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
question: A key-value service handles 50,000 requests per second per machine, shares cores with other services, and runs on laptops for development. Should it adopt DPDK?
options: Probably not: per-request kernel overhead is a tiny part of its budget, and bypass would burn dedicated cores, need root-level device setup and lose kernel tooling
Yes, bypass always lowers latency
Yes, but only with UIO to avoid needing an IOMMU
Yes, because hugepages alone will double its throughput
explain: At 50k requests per second each request has about 20 us of one core, so saving a microsecond of kernel path is noise. Bypass pays off near line rate, not for ordinary services.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
question: A fused kernel for a long row-wise reduction starts spilling registers and runs slower than two unfused kernels. Which fix matches what FlashAttention and Triton tutorials do?
options: Tile the reduction so each block of the row fits on chip, carrying running statistics between tiles
Fuse even more ops into the kernel
Switch to FP64 to get more registers
Disable the GPU's L2 cache
explain: Fusion is bounded by on-chip capacity. Tiling with running statistics (as in FlashAttention's online softmax) keeps the working set small while still avoiding HBM round trips for intermediates.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
question: Two runs differ only in schedule: 30 epochs and 9,600 epochs. Following Beyer et al.'s ImageNet table, which setup should win each run?
options: Function matching wins both; mixup always helps
Consistent teaching wins the short run; function matching wins the long run
The fixed teacher wins the short run, because caching is cheaper per step
All three tie at 9,600 epochs because every student eventually matches the teacher
explain: At 30 epochs consistent teaching leads (74.95% vs 73.89% for function matching). At 9,600 epochs function matching is best (82.31%), consistent teaching close behind (81.76%), and the fixed teacher has overfit (76.95%). Mixup only pays off when there is time to fit the harder inputs.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: An LLM distillation pipeline: logits, tokenizers, traces, compute
question: Your teacher uses a 150k-entry tokenizer and your student a 32k one, but you do have the teacher's full logits. Which option gives a logit-level signal at all?
options: Token-level forward KL after truncating the teacher to 32k entries
Token-level reverse KL, which does not need a shared vocabulary
On-policy GKD with beta = 0.5
ULD: sort both distributions at each position, pad, and penalize the absolute differences
explain: Every KL or JSD variant compares probabilities of the same token, which needs a shared vocabulary; truncating to 32k entries does not make the ids mean the same strings. ULD compares sorted probability vectors, so it only transfers the shape of the distribution, but it works across tokenizers. Seq-KD on generated text is the other option.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
question: A colleague quantizes both keys and values per-token at 2 bits and sees accuracy collapse, while 4-bit per-token worked fine. What is the most likely fix?
options: Use 3-bit per-token for both
Quantize values per-channel and keep keys per-token
Quantize keys per-channel and keep values per-token
Add more calibration data
explain: Per-token key groups get their range stretched by outlier channels, which wipes out the small channels at 2 bits. Per-channel keys fix that. In KIVI's Llama-2-13B test, keys per-token with values per-channel scored 2.80 on CoQA, worse than all per-token.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
question: Using the bars, which move gives the larger capacity gain over GQA-8 BF16: FP8, or keeping 20% of tokens in BF16?
options: FP8, about 2x
They are equal
20% kept, about 5x
Neither changes capacity
explain: FP8 halves bytes per token (59 to 119 sequences). Keeping 20% of tokens cuts per-sequence cache 5x (59 to 297), but with the risk of losing information permanently.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
question: A chatbot has 1,000 active sessions that each return every 5 minutes, and the host tier holds 600 sessions. Under strict LRU, what hit rate should you expect for returning sessions, and why?
options: About 60%, because the tier holds 60% of sessions
100%, because LRU keeps recently active sessions
About 50%, because LRU and FIFO behave the same here
Close to 0%, because each session is the least recently used by the time it returns, so it was just evicted
explain: With a cyclic access pattern larger than the cache, LRU evicts the oldest session, which is exactly the next one to return. Every return misses. Admission filtering that keeps a fixed subset resident, a bigger tier (SSD) or scheduler look-ahead all fix this; matching capacity alone does not.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
question: A node is at (10, 3). It performs a local event when its physical clock reads 11. What timestamp does the event get?
explain: l = max(10, 11) = 11, which differs from the old l, so c resets to 0: (11, 0). The reset is what keeps c bounded: as soon as the physical clock catches up with l, all accumulated ties are forgotten.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Inside the encoders: markers, [MASK] padding and training
question: A user types the 3-word query *who founded pixar*. With the default query length of 32, how many query vectors take part in MaxSim?
options: 3, one per word
4, one per WordPiece token
7, the tokens plus [CLS], [Q] and [SEP]
32, because the query is padded with [MASK] to 32 positions and every position yields a vector
explain: ColBERT pads every query to N_q = 32 with [MASK] tokens, and every position's output vector is used in MaxSim. So the query matrix is always 32 x 128, and the mask vectors act as learned expansion terms.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
question: In one step of ordinary CoT decoding, which operation discards the most information about the model's internal state?
options: The attention layers, because they average over earlier positions
Sampling a single token from softmax(W h), since only its identity is passed on
The final layer normalization before the LM head
The positional encoding added to the next input
explain: The next pass sees only e(x) for the one sampled token, a vector chosen from a fixed table of 50,257 rows. Everything else in the 768-dimensional h(t), including how probable the alternatives were, is dropped. Attention and normalization transform information but pass a full vector on.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why superposition works: continuous thoughts and graph reachability
question: A graph has 30 nodes and diameter 4. In Zhu et al.'s construction, how many continuous thoughts suffice to answer a reachability question about it?
options: 30, one per node
900, one per pair of nodes
5, because log2 of 30 is about 4.9
4, one per step of the diameter
explain: Each thought expands the reachable set by one step along every branch at once, so after D = 4 thoughts every reachable node is in the superposition. 900 echoes the O(n^2) best-known bound for discrete CoT, and 30 is what listing nodes one at a time could need.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
question: Using the same line and bounds (min_err = -1, max_err = +1), you look up key 30, which is not stored. f(30) = 5.41. Which positions do you search, and what lower_bound do you return?
options: Positions 4 to 6; the first key >= 30 is not there, so return not found
Positions 4 to 6; return position 6, the last slot in the window, which holds 26
Only position 5, because the error bound is for stored keys
Positions 4 to 6, then continue right: 41 at position 7 is the lower_bound
explain: The prediction rounds to 5, so the window is 4 to 6, holding 21, 24 and 26, all smaller than 30. The answer sits just past the window edge at position 7. Bounds measured on stored keys say nothing certain about absent keys, so when the search ends at a window boundary you must extend it. Kraska et al. describe exactly this fix.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
question: Your service stores immutable sorted files that are rewritten by background compaction, and lookups are read-heavy. Which learned index design fits most naturally?
options: An ALEX-style updatable index, because data changes over time
A one-pass, error-bounded index (RadixSpline or PGM-style) rebuilt during each compaction
A single deep neural network trained once and never retrained
None: learned indexes cannot be used with files on disk
explain: Each file is written once in sorted order and then never modified, so the model never goes stale for that file. A single-pass build during the merge costs little extra, which is exactly the argument the RadixSpline paper makes for LSM trees.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Training: ranking loss plus the FLOPs regularizer
question: Two terms have the same weight 0.3 in a document. Term A appears in 1 document of the batch, term B in all of them with similar weights. Under FLOPs, which weight is pushed toward zero faster?
options: A, because rare terms are noise
Both equally, since the weights are equal
B, because its mean weight across the batch is larger, so its gradient 2 a_j / N is larger
Neither; FLOPs only acts on queries
explain: The FLOPs gradient for a weight is proportional to the term's batch mean. B is active everywhere, so its posting list is long and its push is strong. L1 would treat A and B the same.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: RankNet: a probability for every pair
question: A pair is correctly ordered with a gap of 6 (sigma = 1). Roughly how big is its push?
options: About 0.0025, close to zero
About 0.5
About 1, the maximum
Exactly 0
explain: Push = 1 / (1 + e^6) = 0.0025. Well-separated, correctly ordered pairs contribute almost nothing, so RankNet focuses on misordered or close pairs. It never reaches exactly 0.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
question: A head has $d_k=64$. A prompt states 500 different key facts, each with its own key direction. What happens to recall under plain linear attention?
options: Nothing, because 500 tokens is short
Keys cannot all be orthogonal in 64 dimensions, so reads mix many stored values
Only the last 64 facts are kept and older ones are cleanly deleted
The model switches to softmax attention automatically
explain: At most 64 directions can be mutually orthogonal. With 500 associations the overlaps $k_i^\top k_j$ are nonzero and every read returns a weighted mixture. Nothing is cleanly deleted either: additive memory never forgets.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Chunkwise DeltaNet derived: WY form and the UT transform by hand
question: Which step of chunkwise DeltaNet keeps a token-by-token dependency inside a chunk?
options: The forward substitution that solves for T
Computing $QK^\top$ for the chunk
Multiplying $T$ by $V$
Computing the masked intra-chunk output
explain: Row r of T depends on rows 1 to r - 1, so forward substitution is inherently ordered, but it is only a C x C system. Everything else is a dense matmul. Across chunks, the state hand-off is the other sequential part.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
question: Which directory would you expect to hold the SSH server's configuration file?
options: /var/log
/proc
/etc
/usr/bin
explain: Configuration local to the machine lives under /etc (the SSH server reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config). /var/log holds logs, /proc is generated live by the kernel, and /usr/bin holds programs.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: sudo and sudoers: controlled, logged use of root
question: What is the main accountability advantage of sudo over sharing the root password for su?
options: sudo is faster
sudo encrypts commands
su cannot run single commands
Each person uses their own password and every command is logged under their name
explain: With su, many people know one secret and logs show only that root did something. sudo authenticates the individual and writes a line per command naming the real user, terminal and command.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
question: sshd ignores alice's authorized_keys even though the key is correct. alice's home directory is mode 777. Why?
options: Ed25519 keys require mode 777
StrictModes refuses keys when the user's files or home directory are writable by others
The file must be owned by root
sshd only reads keys from /etc/ssh
explain: With a world-writable home directory any user could replace .ssh/authorized_keys. StrictModes (default yes) checks ownership and modes before trusting the file, so fix the permissions: home not writable by others, .ssh 700, authorized_keys 600.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: A basic hardening checklist and where to practise
question: You can make one change today on an internet-facing server that still allows SSH passwords and has 30 user accounts. Which change removes the most risk?
options: Set PasswordAuthentication no after giving every user a key
Change the SSH port
Delete /var/log/auth.log to save space
Set umask 000
explain: Thirty passwords means thirty chances that one is weak or reused, and guessing is constant on the internet. Keys remove online guessing entirely. A different port only reduces noise; deleting logs and umask 000 make things worse.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tailoring, exceptions and rolling a baseline out safely
question: Your profile requires `kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 1`. A host reports 2. Is it compliant?
options: Yes: any non-zero value disables unprivileged BPF, so 2 is at least as strong
Yes: 2 is the stricter value
The sysctl does not exist
No: 2 also disables unprivileged BPF now, but an admin can turn it back on later, while 1 cannot be undone until reboot
explain: Both values block unprivileged bpf() today. The difference is reversibility: 1 is one-way until reboot, 2 can be changed back. Whether to accept 2 is a tailoring decision; a strict check makes you take it on purpose.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
question: Why is `-e 2` placed as the last rule rather than the first?
options: It makes auditd start faster
It locks the configuration, so every rule must already be loaded before it runs
augenrules requires it alphabetically
It enables the b32 rules
explain: Once the configuration is locked, no rule can be added or removed until reboot. Rules after it would fail to load. augenrules moves the last -e to the bottom for this reason.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss
question: A host has a userland rootkit that hooks libc to hide a process. Which source still shows that process?
options: ps run in an SSH session on that host
ls /proc in an SSH session on that host
netstat on that host
An eBPF sensor recording sched_process_exec in the kernel
explain: The hooked library lies to programs that call it, and shells spawned on the host are injected. The eBPF program reads kernel events, which the userland hooks never touch.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings
question: Why might a team running eBPF sensors still prefer a scheduled reboot to a livepatch for a non-urgent kernel fix?
options: Livepatch requires disabling lockdown
Livepatch only works on ARM
Per the kernel docs, kprobes in the original function are ignored once calls are redirected, so a sensor probing a patched function can silently stop seeing it
Reboots are faster than livepatches
explain: The livepatch documentation lists this limitation. It is a good reason to livepatch only when the risk demands it and to reboot into the fixed kernel in the next window.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
question: A team has 2,000 queries and 40 ranker variants per week, and wants NDCG@10 for all of them. What is the main reason they consider an LLM judge?
options: NDCG cannot be computed from human labels
Each new variant surfaces unjudged documents, and human labels for all of them are too slow and costly
LLM labels are always more accurate than human labels
LLMs can compute NDCG directly without labels
explain: NDCG needs a grade for every returned document. New rankers keep surfacing unjudged documents, so the labelling bill grows with every experiment. The LLM judge makes that bill small. Accuracy is not automatic: it has to be checked against gold labels.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
question: A colleague adds an "include more detail" step to the generator in a RAG system, and the LLM judge's preference for its answers rises from 50% to 70%. Which explanation should you rule out before celebrating?
options: Verbosity bias: the judge may be rewarding length rather than better content
Position bias in the generator
Kendall's tau is too low
The gold set is too large
explain: Zheng et al.'s repetitive list attack shows weaker judges preferring padded answers over 90% of the time. Check with length-controlled comparisons or human spot checks before attributing the gain to quality.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
question: Which mitigation targets position bias specifically?
options: Using a judge from a different model family
Fitting a tanh length term
Evaluating both orders and combining the results
Adding a reference answer to the prompt
explain: Balanced Position Calibration (Wang et al.) and swap-and-tie (Zheng et al.) run both orders so that position effects cancel or show up as ties. A different-family judge targets self-preference; the length term targets verbosity.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Threat model: how an LLM app gets attacked or goes wrong
question: An email assistant reads the user's inbox and can send emails. Which threat is the most direct route to it sending data to an attacker?
options: A jailbreak typed by the user
Hallucinated claims in a summary
Indirect prompt injection in an incoming email
A slow model response
explain: The attacker only needs to send an email: the assistant reads it as context, and injected instructions plus a send-email tool give a path to exfiltration. A user jailbreak needs the user to be the attacker; hallucination does not move data out.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Measuring a guard, and why no guard is complete
question: A vendor reports their jailbreak detector blocks 99% of attacks in a public benchmark. What is the most important question before relying on it?
options: Which GPU it runs on
Whether it uses a transformer
How it performs against adaptive attacks crafted against it, and what its false positive rate is on your traffic
Whether the benchmark is in English
explain: Static benchmarks measure known attacks. Studies such as Zou et al. and Hackett et al. show optimized or obfuscated inputs evade guards, and the FPR on your own base rate decides how many real users get blocked.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
question: Paging lets a server admit a request after allocating only its prompt's blocks. What new problem does this create that max-length reservation did not have?
options: Requests can no longer share a batch
The pool can run out in the middle of generation, when running requests need new blocks that are not there
Prompts longer than one block cannot be stored
Block tables use more memory than the KV cache itself
explain: Reservation guaranteed every admitted request could finish. Allocating on demand bets that not everyone will grow at once; when the bet loses, some running request has nowhere to put its next token. Handling that is the job of preemption, the next lesson.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
question: With manual chain-of-thought, your code needs only the final number. What does Anthropic suggest?
options: Ask for the answer first, then the reasoning
Forbid reasoning so the output is just the number
Ask for reasoning first and the final answer inside <answer> tags, then extract the tags
Parse the last number that appears anywhere in the response
explain: Reasoning first keeps the benefit; a fixed delimiter makes extraction reliable. Answer-first loses the benefit, and grabbing the last number breaks as soon as the model mentions a number after its answer.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
question: LangChain's default few-shot prompt includes the question *What are songs that were not published on Spotify* for a data source whose only fields are artist, length and genre. What filter does the example answer give?
options: and(ne("platform", "Spotify"))
NO_FILTER, because no field records the platform
not(contain("artist", "Spotify"))
It refuses to answer the query
explain: The example answer is query "" with filter NO_FILTER. The prompt also instructs the model that filters may only refer to attributes that exist. Inventing a platform field would produce a query the store cannot run, or one that silently matches nothing.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
question: To benefit from prompt prefix caching, where should the user's query go in the parser prompt?
options: At the end, after the instructions, field descriptions and examples
At the start, so the model reads it first
In the middle, between instructions and examples
It does not matter, caching hashes the whole prompt
explain: Caching reuses a matching prefix, so everything identical across requests should come first and the part that changes every time should come last. A query at the start changes the prefix on every request and nothing is reused.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
question: Why does the relative saving of FIRST shrink when passages get longer?
options: Longer passages make the first-token logits less accurate
FIRST must generate more tokens for long passages
Prefill grows with L while the decode time saved stays the same, so the saved share falls
Long passages force smaller windows
explain: The saved part is (t_id m - 1) x TPOT, which does not depend on L. Prefill, which both methods pay, grows with mL.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
question: Two passages get p(Yes) = 0.83 and 0.79 from separate calls. Why might the lower one still be the better passage?
options: Each score is produced in isolation, so small differences reflect calibration noise rather than a real comparison
p(Yes) is always inversely related to relevance
Sorting requires scores to sum to 1
The second call used fewer tokens
explain: The model never saw the two passages side by side. Its probability depends on passage length, wording and prompt quirks, so a 0.04 gap is not a reliable comparison. Pairwise and listwise prompts address exactly this.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
question: Why did RankGPT's distilled 440M DeBERTa reranker beat its ChatGPT teacher on BEIR?
options: It was trained on human relevance labels as well
It ranks each passage with a stable deterministic score instead of an occasionally malformed or inconsistent permutation
It used a longer context window than ChatGPT
It reranked 1000 passages instead of 100
explain: The student learns the teacher's preferences through a pairwise RankNet loss but scores each passage with a deterministic forward pass, so it avoids the teacher's missing ids, repetitions and window-to-window inconsistency. The authors attribute the gap to this stability.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail
question: After launching in Japan, your router's share of strong-model calls drops from 35% to 12% and complaints about answer quality rise. What is the most likely cause?
options: The strong model became cheaper
Input distribution shift: the router misjudges the difficulty of prompts unlike its training data and sends hard ones to the weak model
Judge bias toward longer answers
The router's GPU is overloaded
explain: A sudden change in routing mix plus worse quality right after new traffic arrives points to drift. Bedrock's docs say its routing is optimized only for English prompts, and RouteLLM's routers fell to near random on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
question: Inlier ratio is 0.5 and you need 99% confidence. How many RANSAC iterations does a homography (s = 4) need?
explain: N = log(0.01)/log(1 - 0.5^4) = log(0.01)/log(0.9375) = 71.36, rounded up to 72. 16 is 1/w^4, the expected number of draws to see the first clean sample, which is not enough for 99% confidence. 567 is the answer for w = 0.3.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
question: A thread in enqueue reads Tail = X and finds X.next is not NULL. What does the algorithm do?
options: Wait until the thread that linked X.next swings Tail
Try to CAS Tail forward to X.next, then retry its own enqueue
Link its node after X anyway
Return failure because the queue is full
explain: That is E13: Tail is lagging, so the thread helps advance it and loops. Waiting would make the algorithm blocking, and linking after X would break the list because X is not the last node.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
question: Why is "88 percent of Thunderbird's templates are missing from a 2,000-line sample" a problem for a hand-written regex set, but not fatal for a template miner?
options: The miner has already seen all 1,241 templates during training
The miner stores raw lines, so it can re-derive templates on demand
The miner creates a new template group the first time it sees an unmatched line, so unseen formats cost nothing extra
Rare templates are noise and a miner correctly discards them
explain: An online miner's whole job is to open a new group for a line that matches nothing. A regex set has to be edited by a person before the new format parses at all, and until then those lines fall into an unparsed bucket. Rare templates are usually the valuable ones: error-level messages are rare by construction.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
question: Your log volume quadruples and the parser falls behind. Which of the Huawei deployment's four measures gives both a throughput win and an accuracy win?
options: Partitioning by verbosity level and component, since different levels and components come from different logging statements: fewer candidates per partition, and the partitions parse in parallel
Raising the similarity threshold so fewer comparisons are needed
Reducing the tree depth to shorten every walk
Sampling one line in four and extrapolating the counts
explain: Partitioning narrows the search space, which speeds parsing, and it also removes the chance of merging templates across components, which helps accuracy. It is also the parallelization key they used with Spark. Threshold and depth are accuracy trade-offs, not free wins, and sampling destroys exactly the rare error templates you most want to count.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
question: At Equifax, what would most directly have shortened the 76 days?
options: A new Sigma rule for Struts exploits
An alert when an inspection device stops decrypting (expired certificate) or its sensors stop producing alerts
Longer log retention
Moving the IDS in front of the SSLV device
explain: The detection layer was fine once it could see. What failed was visibility, and nothing alerted on its loss. Monitoring sensor health (and owning certificate renewal) attacks the actual cause. An IDS in front of the decryptor would see only ciphertext.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: MITRE ATT&CK as a coverage map
question: A rule's tag is attack.t1059.001. What does it tell another engineer?
options: The rule's severity
Which ATT&CK sub-technique (PowerShell, under Command and Scripting Interpreter) the rule is meant to detect
The rule's Sigma version
The Windows event ID it reads
explain: Sigma tags use the attack namespace for ATT&CK. T1059.001 is the PowerShell sub-technique; tags let tools build coverage maps automatically.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Tuning and allowlisting without blinding yourself
question: A rule's alert count drops from 40 a day to 0 after a tuning change. What should you check first?
options: That the rule's must-match test cases still pass, and that the data source is still arriving
Nothing, the tuning worked perfectly
The SIEM licence
Whether analysts are happy
explain: Zero is suspicious. Either the filter is too broad (tests catch that), or the source went silent (pipeline health catches that). Both look like success.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
question: In the toy head (wavelengths 6.3, 62.8, 628.3, 6,283 tokens; trained on 2,048), which pair sees an out-of-distribution angle first as the prompt grows past 2,048 tokens?
options: Pair 0, because it rotates fastest and accumulates the largest angle
Pair 3, because it never completed a full turn during training
All pairs equally, because every position past 2,048 is new
None, because RoPE only depends on relative distance
explain: Pair 0 reaches huge raw angles but wraps every 6.3 tokens, so every angle on its circle was seen thousands of times. Pair 3 only ever covered 0 to 2.047 rad, so at position 2,100 it is already at 2.1 rad, outside its training range.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
question: Why does DeepSpeed Ulysses' per-link communication stay constant as you scale sequence length and GPU count together?
options: It compresses activations to 1 bit
It only communicates the KV cache once per training run
It never communicates; each GPU attends locally
An all-to-all over P GPUs moves M/P per link, and the message M = 4Nh grows with N at the same rate as P
explain: Per-link volume is 4Nh/P. Doubling both N and P leaves it unchanged. With h = 4096 and N = 32K tokens per GPU, that is about 1.07 GB per layer in bf16 at P = 2, 4, 8 or 16.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
question: Yang et al. train a looped transformer without input injection (Y_(t+1) = M(Y_t), Y_0 = P). What did they observe when running more loops than in training?
options: Error kept falling, because more loops always help
Error was unchanged, because the state had converged
Error grew quickly (diverged) past the trained loop count
The model refused to run more loops
explain: Without re-injecting the prompt, the influence of the start fades and the state drifts once the loop count leaves the trained range. With injection, the end point stays tied to the input, which is the same reason Huginn feeds e into every iteration.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
question: For k = 8, Saunshi et al. report open-book QA scores of 33.9 (24 layers), 22.7 (8 layers) and 30.8 (8 layers looped 3x). What is the % Gap?
options: About 24%
About 51%
About 72%
About 136%
explain: (30.8 - 22.7) / (33.9 - 22.7) = 8.1 / 11.2 = 0.72, about 72%, matching the paper's table. The looped model recovers most of the missing parameters' benefit on this context-reasoning group.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Counting parameters, choosing targets, merging for free inference
question: You add a rank-8 LoRA to one MLP up-projection of shape 4096 by 11008. How many trainable parameters does that adapter have?
explain: r(d + k) = 8 x (4096 + 11008) = 8 x 15104 = 120,832. 65,536 would be a square 4096 matrix, and 45,088,768 is the full matrix itself.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
question: What does slicing cost in exchange for faster unlearning?
options: Lower accuracy, because each slice model is a weaker learner
Storage, because parameters must be checkpointed before every slice
Privacy, because checkpoints leak the deleted point
Nothing, slicing is free
explain: Slicing changes when data is added inside a shard, not how much data a model sees, so the paper reports no accuracy cost. The overhead is storing the parameter state before each slice is introduced so that retraining can resume from the last checkpoint that never saw the point. Old checkpoints that contain the point must be discarded after unlearning.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
question: A file arrives as an email attachment, shows a fake invoice, does not copy itself anywhere, and silently downloads a second program from the internet. Which labels fit best?
options: Worm and wiper
Virus and rootkit
Trojan and loader
Worm and ransomware
explain: It looks benign and does not replicate (trojan), and its job is fetching other malware (loader). A worm would spread to other machines on its own; a virus would infect other files.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Reading x86-64 assembly: registers and core instructions
question: Which register holds a function's integer return value on x86-64?
options: rsp
rcx
rax
rip
explain: rax (or its low half eax) carries the return value. rsp is the stack pointer, rcx carries the first argument on Windows, and rip points at the next instruction.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Command and control: beacons, jitter and Cobalt Strike
question: A Beacon checks in every 300 seconds with 20% jitter. Which set of gaps between check-ins is consistent with Fortra's documentation?
explain: With 20% jitter the documented range is 240 to 300 seconds. Only the first set stays in that window.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Sharing intelligence and writing the analysis report
question: In TLP 2.0, what does TLP:AMBER+STRICT allow?
options: Sharing only within the recipient's own organisation
Public sharing
Sharing with the whole community but not the press
Sharing only with named individuals in the meeting
explain: FIRST's standard: AMBER allows the recipient's organisation and its clients on a need-to-know basis; AMBER+STRICT restricts sharing to the organisation only.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Why one GPU cannot train a 175B model, and the five ways to split it
question: A team has a 1.3B model (about 23 GB of model state at 18 bytes per parameter) that fits on one 80 GB GPU with its activations, and wants to train faster on 64 GPUs. Following the Megatron guidance, what should they try first?
options: TP=8 so every layer is split as finely as possible
Plain data parallelism (DP=64), adding model parallelism only if memory runs out
PP=64 so each GPU holds one or two layers
CP=64 so each GPU holds a sliver of each sequence
explain: The Megatron Core guide says to start with data parallelism and add TP, then PP, only when the model does not fit. Model parallelism adds communication and makes per-GPU matrix multiplies smaller, so it is a cost you pay for memory, not a free speedup.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
question: Two runs of the same model on the same GPUs both report 160 TFLOP/s per GPU. Run A uses full recompute, run B uses selective recompute. Which trains faster in tokens per second?
options: Run A, because full recompute frees memory for larger batches
They are the same, the TFLOP/s are equal
Run B, because fewer of its FLOPs are wasted on recomputation, so more go to useful model FLOPs
It cannot be decided without knowing the vocabulary size
explain: Both execute FLOPs at the same rate, but A spends about a quarter of them redoing the forward pass. B's model FLOPs per second, and so its MFU and tokens per second, are higher. This is exactly the HFU vs MFU distinction.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: An image is not a photograph: smear, footprint and checks
question: A socket's creation time in the image is 22 seconds later than the image's SystemTime. Which explanation fits best?
options: The socket was created by the analyst's machine
The clock page was copied before the page holding the socket, because acquisition took tens of seconds
Windows clocks run backwards during dumps
netscan converts times to local time
explain: SystemTime reflects the moment its page was copied, not the end of acquisition. Later pages can hold objects created after that moment.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: VADs and malfind: finding code that has no file
question: Why are code regions from normally loaded DLLs not reported by malfind?
options: Because DLLs are never executable
Because malfind only scans the kernel
Because the loader encrypts DLLs in memory
They are mapped image files with PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY protection, which malfind's rule excludes
explain: Image mappings get EXECUTE_WRITECOPY. malfind wants private executable memory or a mapping with some other protection, which normal loading does not create.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Cobalt Strike Beacon in memory: finding and reading its configuration
question: Your YARA rules for Beacon match nothing in an image, but netscan shows rundll32.exe with regular HTTPS connections to a rare host. What fits Fortra's documentation?
options: Beacon never runs in rundll32.exe
YARA cannot read memory images
Sleep masks delete the network objects
The Beacon may have been masked by its sleep mask at capture time, so absence of a match is not absence of Beacon
explain: The default sleep mask obfuscates Beacon while sleeping. Pivot to the process's threads, sockets and unmasked code, consider a second capture, and use tools built for masked process dumps.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Case: Ivanti Connect Secure, and a memory-first workflow
question: A VPN appliance is confirmed compromised. Following Volexity's advice, what comes first?
options: Wipe and rebuild immediately to stop the attacker
Collect logs, a system snapshot, and memory and disk images before wiping or rebuilding, then hunt for lateral movement
Apply the patch and close the case
Reboot the appliance to clear in-memory implants
explain: Patching and rebuilding do not reveal past compromise, and a reboot destroys memory evidence. Collect first, then contain, then hunt from the device inward.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
question: A Redis instance reports mem_fragmentation_ratio 2.1, with used_memory 40 MB and RSS 84 MB. What should you do?
options: Probably nothing: 44 MB of absolute overhead is small and includes code and libraries
Enable activedefrag immediately
Restart the instance to reset fragmentation
Lower dirty_decay_ms to 0
explain: The Redis docs warn that a high ratio with only a few megabytes of difference is not an issue: the ratio also counts code, shared libraries and stacks, which dominate a small instance. Check allocator_frag_bytes before acting.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: SeqCst, fences, and when you need one global order
question: Why does `Arc::drop` use Release on every `fetch_sub`, rather than only on the one that reaches zero?
options: Because Release makes the decrement faster on x86
Because no thread knows in advance whether its decrement is the last, and every non-final owner's uses must happen-before the deletion
Because fetch_sub cannot be Relaxed
Because SeqCst is required for reference counts
explain: Whichever thread frees the data needs a happens-before edge from every other owner's last use. Each non-final owner provides that by releasing on its decrement; the final owner acquires (via the fence) before deleting. The Acquire is only needed by the one thread that sees old == 1.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
question: N = 8 threads, K = 2 hazard pointers each, R = 2H. What is the maximum number of retired-but-unfreed nodes, and the minimum freed per scan?
options: 16 and 8
32 and 16
128 and 8
explain: H = N x K = 16, so R = 32. The bound is N x R = 8 x 32 = 256 waiting nodes. Each scan checks 32 nodes and at most 16 can be protected, so it frees at least R minus H = 16.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
question: A function keeps a pointer to a buffer, frees the buffer, and an hour later reads through the pointer. Which family is this?
options: Temporal: the read happens after the object's lifetime ended
Spatial: the read is past the end of the buffer
Type: the buffer is read as the wrong type
Not a memory safety bug, since the address is still valid
explain: The address is the same one that was once valid, so it is not about bounds. It is about time: the object no longer exists and the memory may belong to something else now. That is a temporal bug, usually called use-after-free.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Out-of-bounds reads: Heartbleed and why leaks matter
question: Why could Heartbleed leak private keys even though the bug never wrote to memory?
options: It replaced the key with a known value
TLS sends keys in heartbeats
It crashed the server so keys were dumped to disk
It copied up to 64 KB of whatever was next to the heartbeat buffer into the reply, and server memory held keys and passwords
explain: An over-read copies neighbouring memory out. Whatever the server process had in memory near that buffer, including key material and other users' data, could appear in the reply. No write and no crash was needed.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Uninitialized memory and type confusion
question: Which is the best fix for show() in the tagged-union example?
options: Cast `v->u.num` to a pointer explicitly
Switch on `v->kind` and read only the member the tag names; reject unknown tags
Make the union bigger
Catch the crash with a signal handler
explain: The bug is reading a member the tag does not vouch for. Checking the tag first removes the confusion; casting just hides it, and catching the crash leaves a chosen-address read possible.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
question: With contrastive loss and margin m = 1, a dissimilar pair sits at distance D = 0.4. What is its loss?
explain: The dissimilar term is 0.5 x max(0, 1 - 0.4)^2 = 0.5 x 0.36 = 0.18. If the pair were at D = 1.2 the loss would be 0.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: When the optimizer deletes the code you meant to time
question: A colleague's benchmark reports 0.25 ns per call for a function that parses a 40-byte string. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The compiler removed or folded the work, so the loop no longer parses anything
The parser is vectorized and handles many bytes per cycle
The timer has 1 ns resolution, so the number is rounded down
The string fits in L1 cache, so parsing is nearly free
explain: Parsing 40 bytes cannot finish in about one clock cycle, even with vector instructions and a warm L1 cache. Timer resolution is not the issue either: the total time is divided by many iterations. An impossible per-call time almost always means the result was unused (dead code) or the input was a compile-time constant (folding).

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
question: Mytkowicz et al. found that link order alone moved perlbench's -O3 speedup between 0.92 and 1.10. What does that imply for a single-build comparison of two compiler flags?
options: Only that more repetitions are needed
Link order matters only for programs as large as perlbench
A single build is one sample of memory layout, so its result can favor either flag regardless of how many times it is run
The Core 2 was faulty
explain: Each point in their data was reproducible across runs, so repetitions do not help: the bias is fixed by the build's layout. Stabilizer's authors put it directly: a single binary is one sample from the space of program layouts. Mytkowicz et al. saw such effects on every machine they tried, including a simulator.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
question: Which run gains nothing from --use-rollout-routing-replay?
options: A GRPO run on Qwen3-30B-A3B with FP8 rollout
A multi-turn agentic run on a 744B MoE
A GRPO run on dense Qwen3-4B
A GSPO run on GLM-4.7-Flash
explain: R3 replays expert routing. A dense model has no router, so there is nothing to record or replay. The other three are MoE models where routing can flip between rollout and training.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
question: The boundary is 1M requests. Which training target choice best fits what LRB needs to get right?
options: log(time to next request), so the error between 100K and 2M counts more than between 2M and 3M
Raw time to next request with L2 loss, so large values dominate the loss
A binary label, recently used or not
The number of past requests
explain: The model only has to decide which side of the boundary an object falls on and rank the candidates. On a log scale a 20x error near the boundary is large while a 1.5x error far beyond it is small. The paper tried raw time, binary classification and other targets; log time gave the highest good decision ratio.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Inside an APK and an IPA: what anyone can download and read
question: You copy an App Store app's main binary from a jailbroken iPhone and open it in a disassembler, but the code section looks like random bytes. What is the most likely reason?
options: iOS binaries are compressed with ZIP
Swift code cannot be disassembled
The app is obfuscated by default by Xcode
App Store binaries are encrypted with Apple's DRM, so a decrypted copy must be dumped from memory while the app runs, or obtained from the developer
explain: The MASTG notes that because of DRM the binary is encrypted when stored on the device; pulling it from the bundle is not enough. The IPA is a ZIP, but the binary inside it is the encrypted part. Xcode does not obfuscate by default, and Swift binaries disassemble like any other.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Android IPC: exported components, intent redirection, PendingIntents
question: Why did the EngageSDK flaw affect apps whose developers never wrote an exported activity?
options: Because Android exports every activity by default since Android 12
Because the SDK modified the app's code at runtime
Because the library's own manifest added an exported activity to each app's merged manifest during the build
Because Google Play exports components after upload
explain: Microsoft explains that MTCommonActivity was added to the merged manifest when the library was imported, appearing only after the build, which is why developers missed it. Android 12 made the exported attribute mandatory for components with intent filters; it did not export everything.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The app is not the boundary: backend APIs seen through the app
question: A tester toggles 'hide my age' in a dating app, then checks their own profile through the proxy from a second test account. The screen shows no age, but the JSON has `"birth_year": 1994`. How should this be reported?
options: As server-side excessive data exposure: the API ignores the privacy setting and sends the field anyway
Not a finding, since the app hides it correctly
As a client-side rendering bug to be fixed in the app
As a certificate pinning failure, because the proxy could read it
explain: The setting must be enforced where the data leaves the server; any client, including a script, receives the field. It is OWASP API3 (Broken Object Property Level Authorization, its excessive data exposure half) and a MASVS-PRIVACY concern. The proxy only made it visible; the tester used their own lab setup and two accounts they control.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head
question: In DeepSeek-V3, which tensors does an MLA layer write to the KV cache for each new token?
options: The per-head keys $k^C$ and values $v^C$
The query latent $c^Q$ and the key latent $c^{KV}$
The layer input $h_t$, since everything can be recomputed from it
The key-value latent $c^{KV}$ and the shared RoPE key $k^R$
